trivia_fact: The PersistentVolume (PV) and PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) separation was inspired by cloud volume APIs. PVs represent actual storage resources (like an AWS EBS volume), while PVCs are requests for storage. This abstraction lets developers request storage without knowing the underlying infrastructure.

The Container Storage Interface (CSI) was created to standardize how container orchestrators interact with storage systems. Before CSI, storage drivers were compiled directly into Kubernetes ("in-tree"), requiring a Kubernetes release for every driver update. CSI made drivers independently deployable.

Container storage is ephemeral by default in Kubernetes — when a pod dies, its filesystem vanishes. This is intentional, not a limitation. It enforces the principle that pods are disposable and state should be explicitly managed through PersistentVolumes.

A StorageClass acts as a "provisioner profile" that defines what kind of storage to create (SSD vs HDD, replicated vs local, etc.). When a PVC references a StorageClass, Kubernetes automatically provisions matching storage — this is called dynamic provisioning, and it eliminated manual PV creation.

The emptyDir volume type creates a temporary directory that exists only as long as the pod runs. It can be backed by disk or RAM (tmpfs). Its most common use is sharing files between containers in the same pod — like a sidecar writing logs that another container ships.

ConfigMaps and Secrets can be mounted as volumes in pods, making configuration files appear in the container filesystem. Updates to ConfigMaps are eventually propagated to mounted volumes without pod restarts, though the propagation delay can be up to a minute.

PersistentVolumes have a reclaim policy that controls what happens when a PVC is deleted. "Retain" keeps the data for manual cleanup, "Delete" removes the underlying storage (common in cloud), and "Recycle" (deprecated) used to do a basic rm -rf on the volume.

Local PersistentVolumes, added in Kubernetes 1.14 (GA), let you use local disks (NVMe SSDs, etc.) as persistent storage with the PV/PVC abstraction. The scheduler becomes topology-aware — it only schedules pods to nodes where the local volume actually exists.

CSI Volume Snapshots (GA in Kubernetes 1.20) brought point-in-time copy capability to Kubernetes storage. Inspired by cloud provider snapshot APIs, they let you create a VolumeSnapshot object that captures the state of a PVC, which can then be used to create new volumes or restore data.

PersistentVolumes support three access modes: ReadWriteOnce (single node), ReadOnlyMany (multiple nodes read), and ReadWriteMany (multiple nodes read-write). Not all storage backends support all modes — for example, AWS EBS only supports ReadWriteOnce because it can only attach to one EC2 instance at a time.
